---
title: "Identity & profiles"
description: "Your identity is a key: profile files, slots, portability, and what none of it attests."
---

EOS Reimagined has no accounts, no logins, and no server that knows who you are. **A profile is a
key**: on first run the library generates an X25519 keypair and keeps it in a small file. Your
player IDs are *derived* from its public half, and its private half is what proves them to other
players — every connection runs a [Noise XX handshake](../developers/internals/adr/0001-authenticated-mesh-identity.qmd),
and a peer is adopted under the identity *recomputed from the key it proved*, never under
anything it merely claims.

## The profile file

The key lives in your [data directory](configuration.qmd#where-the-file-lives) as `profile.key` —
a comment header plus one line holding 64 hex characters:

```
# EOS Reimagined profile. This key is your identity: keep it secret, and
# back it up -- there is nobody who can reissue it.
key 4f3a…                                     # 64 lowercase hex characters
```

Three facts follow directly:

- **Copy the file, carry the player.** Move `profile.key` to another machine (it survives
  Windows ↔ Linux round-trips, CRLF and all) and you are the same player there. The file *is*
  the export format.
- **Keep it secret.** Anyone holding the file can *be* you on the mesh — treat it like an SSH
  private key. It is written owner-only (`0600` on Linux; per-user AppData ACLs on Windows).
- **Back it up.** There is no recovery authority. Losing the file loses the identity; the library
  will mint a fresh one and other players will see a new player.

Don't run the *same* profile on two machines at once: the design de-duplicates copies on one
machine, but two machines wearing one key are one player, and the mesh will refuse the second
connection claiming an already-connected identity.

## Two IDs from one key

The EOS API speaks two identities, and both derive from your profile:

- Your **Epic account ID** (`EOS_EpicAccountId`) is product-independent — the same across every
  game, like an account.
- Your **product user ID** (`EOS_ProductUserId`) also folds in the game's product, sandbox, and
  deployment IDs — so one profile is a *distinct* product-user per title, exactly matching EOS
  semantics.

Both keep the standard 32-hex format games expect. And because the game's own IDs are part of the
derivation *and* the handshake, two different games on one LAN don't just ignore each other —
they cannot complete a handshake at all.

## Profile slots: couch co-op that just works

Several copies of a game on one machine must be several *players* — if they shared one profile
they would derive one ID, see each other's advertisements as their own, and never mesh. So each
running instance claims an **exclusive profile slot** in the data directory:

```
profile.key    profile.lock      # slot 0 — first instance
profile-1.key  profile-1.lock    # slot 1 — second instance
…
profile-9.key  profile-9.lock    # slot 9 — tenth instance
```

A slot is held by an OS-level file lock (`flock` on Linux, exclusive open on Windows) for the
life of the process:

- The lock **dies with the process**, so a crash never strands a slot.
- A given instance lands on the **same slot — and the same identity — every run** (first free
  slot wins, and your usual instance count is stable).
- Ten slots, matching the ten [discovery ports](networking.qmd): at most ten meshing instances
  per data directory.

A launcher that wants deterministic identities (Nucleus-style co-op orchestration) shouldn't rely
on slot order at all — give each instance its own `EOSR_DATA_DIR`, and each directory gets its
own `profile.key` at slot 0:

```sh
EOSR_DATA_DIR=~/eosr/p1 ./game &   # always Alice
EOSR_DATA_DIR=~/eosr/p2 ./game &   # always Bob
```

## Edge behavior worth knowing

- **No writable directory is not fatal.** If the library can't write anywhere (or every slot is
  taken), the instance keeps the ephemeral key it started with and notes that the identity will
  not outlive the run. The mesh still works; only persistence is lost.
- **A corrupt or all-zero profile is replaced,** never adopted — a truncated key file can't
  silently become a shared or degenerate identity.
- **Your display name is just a name.** It travels as metadata and can be changed freely in
  [`eosr.json`](configuration.qmd); it has no part in your identity. (It used to seed identity in
  older emulator designs — which meant anyone typing your name *became* you. That is exactly what
  the key design removes.)
- **`epicid` / `productuserid` config keys are refused** for the same reason — an ID you merely
  claim would be rejected by exactly the peers it was meant to reach. See
  [Configuration](configuration.qmd#keys-from-other-emulators).

## What this does — and does not — attest

What the mesh authenticates is **key possession**: nobody can answer to your identity without
holding your file, no frame can be forged or replayed, and a connection is a peer or it is
nothing. That is the strongest thing a backendless emulator can honestly offer, and it is
enough to make owner/participant checks in sessions and lobbies real.

What it can never attest is that an identity belongs to a **real Epic account** or a
**legitimate game owner**. That would require Epic (or another trusted authority), and this
project does not pretend to it — see [Scope & non-goals](scope.qmd).
